notes.meaning: Paul and Silas traveled along the main Roman highway through Amphipolis and Apollonia until they reached Thessalonica. Thessalonica was a bustling seaport and capital city with an established Jewish synagogue. Because a synagogue was already there, it gave the missionaries a natural place to begin preaching.

Paul followed his regular habit of taking the good news to the Jewish people first. For three weeks in a row on the Sabbath, he went to the synagogue and held discussions based on the Scriptures. He engaged the people in friendly dialogue, answering questions and pointing them to God's word.

Paul carefully opened up the Old Testament prophecies to show that the promised Messiah had to suffer, die, and rise from the dead. Many expected a political conqueror, so Paul explained why the cross was necessary. He then announced that Jesus of Nazareth is this very Messiah.

Some of the Jewish listeners were persuaded by Paul's teaching and joined the missionary team. A large group of Greek worshippers who honored God also believed, along with many leading women of the city. God used this message to bring together people from different backgrounds into one new family of faith.

The Jewish leaders who rejected the message became jealous of the large crowds following Paul and Silas. They recruited rough, idle men hanging around the public square to start an angry mob and create chaos in the city. The mob then marched to the house of Jason, hoping to drag the apostles out to the crowd.

When the angry crowd could not find Paul and Silas, they dragged Jason and several other local Christians before the city rulers instead. They shouted that these preachers were causing disturbances all over the Roman world. Without realizing it, the accusers showed just how powerful the gospel had become.

The mob claimed Jason was guilty because he welcomed these traveling preachers into his home. To make the matter seem serious to Roman officials, they accused the believers of treason against Caesar by declaring that Jesus is King. The accusers twisted the spiritual truth about Jesus into a political threat.

Hearing reports of rebellion against the emperor alarmed both the crowd and the city rulers. The magistrates knew Rome had zero tolerance for riots or disloyalty, and they feared getting into trouble with the imperial government. An atmosphere of panic quickly spread through the assembly.

The city leaders required Jason and the other believers to pay a sum of money as bail before releasing them. This financial deposit guaranteed that there would be no more public disturbances and that the peace would be kept. With the bond paid, the officials let the believers go home.

As soon as night arrived, the local Christians sent Paul and Silas away to Berea to keep them safe and protect Jason's pledge. Even after facing violent threats, the missionaries did not stop preaching. Upon arriving in Berea, they went directly to the local Jewish synagogue to share the message again.

The listeners in Berea showed an open and fair-minded attitude toward the new teaching. They welcomed the message with great interest, yet they did not accept it blindly. Every single day, they examined the Old Testament Scriptures to verify whether Paul's teaching matched God's written word.

differ.view: Hold up the Bereans as the model for using Scripture alone as the final authority to test all teaching.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Teach that the Bereans' nobility was their willingness to receive the oral message, using the Old Testament to confirm prophecies rather than practicing Scripture alone.

notes.meaning: Because the Bereans carefully checked the message against the Scriptures, many of them became convinced and believed in Jesus. Their new faith was shared by prominent Greek men and women from the community. Honest searching of God's Word led to genuine faith in Christ.

When Paul's opponents in Thessalonica learned he was having success in Berea, they traveled about fifty miles just to stop him. They began stirring up the crowds and creating unrest, repeating the tactics they had used before. Their fierce opposition showed how much they hated the spread of the gospel.

The Berean believers acted quickly to protect Paul by guiding him toward the coast. Silas and Timothy stayed behind in Berea to teach and strengthen the young church. The team balanced personal safety with caring for the spiritual health of new converts.

The companions traveling with Paul escorted him safely all the way to Athens. Once they arrived, Paul sent them back with an urgent request for Silas and Timothy to rejoin him as soon as possible. Paul valued fellowship and partnership in ministry, especially when facing a new city alone.

While waiting for his partners in Athens, Paul was deeply upset by what surrounded him. Athens was celebrated for its art and wisdom, but statues and altars to pagan gods filled every street corner. Instead of admiring the city's beauty, Paul felt deep sorrow over its widespread idolatry.

Driven by concern for the city, Paul began speaking about the Lord wherever he could find listeners. He debated with Jews and Gentile worshippers in the synagogue, and he spoke in the open marketplace every day with ordinary shoppers and passersby. He took the message straight to the center of daily public life.

Philosophers from two famous groups, the Epicureans and the Stoics, began debating with Paul in the marketplace. Some dismissed him as an untrained babbler, while others thought he was introducing strange foreign gods because he talked about Jesus and the resurrection. Even though they misunderstood him, Paul stayed focused on Christ.

The philosophers invited Paul to the Areopagus, an ancient council and public meeting place on Mars' Hill. They wanted a clear and orderly presentation of the new doctrines he had been teaching. This invitation gave Paul a great platform to address the leading thinkers of Athens.

The council members noted that Paul was bringing ideas they had never heard before. The notion of a bodily resurrection sounded bizarre to their ears, and they wanted a deeper explanation of what it meant. Their curiosity gave Paul a chance to speak plainly about the truth.

The Athenians and the foreign visitors who stayed there were famous for how they spent their time. They loved nothing more than hearing, debating, and repeating the latest theories and news. Yet their constant craving for novel ideas left them blind to the eternal truth of God.

Paul stood up in the center of the Areopagus and addressed the council with dignity and respect. He noted that in every aspect of life, the Athenians were deeply devoted to religious rituals. Rather than starting with an insult, he acknowledged their religious earnestness as a bridge to share the truth.

Paul shared that as he walked through their streets, he found an altar dedicated to an unknown god, built so the city would not overlook any deity. He told them that the very God they worshipped without knowing was the One he had come to proclaim. Paul used their own monument to point them to the true Creator.

Paul declared that the true God created the entire universe and everything inside it. Because He is the sovereign Lord of heaven and earth, He cannot be contained within stone temples made by human hands. This statement directly challenged the idea that gods live inside human-built shrines.

The living God does not need anything from humans, nor does He depend on people to feed or serve Him through rituals. Instead, He is the ultimate Giver who gives life, breath, and every good thing to all living creatures. We depend on Him for every moment, not the other way around.

God created all nations of humanity from one common ancestor, establishing that every person shares the same origin. He also determined the eras of human history and set the geographic boundaries where each people group would live. God actively guides the history and destiny of the world.

God placed people on the earth with the purpose that they would seek Him and reach out to find Him, like someone feeling their way through the dark. Even though people have been blind to Him, God has never been far away from any of us. He desires that everyone come into a relationship with Him.

differ.view: Emphasizes that God leaves the way open to be found by all, offering grace without forcing the human will.

notes.meaning: Human life and movement continue only because God constantly upholds our existence. Paul even cited well-known Greek poets who wrote that humans are God's offspring. He showed his listeners that their own literature recognized humanity's constant dependence on the Creator.

Since humans are created by God with minds and souls, it makes no sense to think the Creator is an object of gold, silver, or carved rock. A statue shaped by human hands can never represent the living God who gave us life. True worship must be directed to the living God, not to handmade images.

In earlier centuries, God showed great patience by overlooking the spiritual ignorance of pagan nations without sending immediate destruction. But now that the good news of Christ has arrived, God commands every person everywhere to repent and turn to Him. The time of making excuses for idolatry has come to an end.

differ.view: Emphasizes that although the command to repent is universal, fallen humans have no natural power to turn to God apart from special enabling grace.
Emphasizes that God's universal command leaves all people fully accountable, stripping away every excuse before His sovereign court.

notes.meaning: God has appointed a specific day when He will judge the entire world with absolute justice through the Man He chose. He gave undeniable proof of this future judgment to all humanity by raising Jesus from the dead. The resurrection guarantees that Christ has the authority to judge all people.

The moment Paul spoke of the resurrection from the dead, some of the philosophers began to laugh and make fun of him. Others in the crowd were more polite and asked to hear him speak on the topic again later. People reacted to the good news in different ways, just as they still do today.

Seeing that the meeting had broken down into mocking and delays, Paul walked away from the council. He did not waste time in fruitless arguments with those who only wanted to ridicule the truth. His departure marked the end of his public address on Mars' Hill.

Even though many mocked, some people joined Paul and believed the message of salvation. These new believers included Dionysius, an influential member of the Areopagus court, along with a woman named Damaris and several others. Even in a proud and skeptical city, God's word bore fruit in receptive hearts.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: Reveres Dionysius as an early bishop of Athens and martyr, and honors Damaris as the first Athenian woman to embrace the Christian faith.
